deep.reconstruction:
The page holds two complete 'Canon'-type tables of indices (discrete logarithms) in the Gaussian integers Z[i]. They belong to Gauss's work on biquadratic residues. Each table has three parts:

(a) a Gaussian prime modulus m of prime norm D = N(m) = p ≡ 1 (mod 4);
(b) the powers g^k of the primitive root g = 1+i for k = 0..(p−1)/4, each reduced to a small-norm residue a+bi;
(c) the indices ind_g(q) of the 'Elementargrössen'.

The Elementargrössen are the unit i together with the Gaussian primes of norm up to about 101. Each is normalised to the associate a+bi with b even and a ≡ 1 (mod 4): i, 1±i, 1±2i, −3, −3±2i, 1±4i, 5±2i, 1±6i, 5±4i, −7, −7±2i, 5±6i, −3±8i, 5±8i, 9±4i, 1±10i.

Why the power table stops at (p−1)/4 [my explanation]: g^{(p−1)/4} ≡ i. Every higher power is therefore i^j times a listed one, and ind(i^j·x) = j(p−1)/4 + ind(x).

Method of checking [my reconstruction]: Z[i]/(m) ≅ Z/p, with i mapped to a square root of −1 mod p.

Modulus m = 1+10i, D = 101:
- From 1+10i ≡ 0 we get i ≡ −1/10 ≡ 10 (mod 101), since 10² = 100 ≡ −1. So g = 1+i ↦ 11.
- 11 is a primitive root mod 101: 11^20 ≡ 87 and 11^50 ≡ −1.
- The powers, as integers mod 101: 1, 11, 20=2i, 18=−2+2i, −4, −44=−4−4i, 21=1+2i, 29=−1+3i, 16=−4+2i, −26=4−3i, 17=−3+2i, −15=−5−i, 37=−3+4i, 3, 33=3+3i, −41=−1−4i, −47=3−5i, −12=−2−i, −31=−1−3i, −38=2−4i, −14=−4−i, 48=−2+5i, 23=3+2i, 51=1+5i, −45=−5−4i, 10=i (k = 25 = 100/4).
- Indices, using ind(−1) = 50 and ind(±i) = 25, 75. Examples:
  - 1−i = −i(1+i), so ind = 75+1 = 76.
  - −3: ind = 50 + ind 3 = 50 + 13 = 63.
  - 1−4i ≡ −39, and 11^45 ≡ −39, so ind = 45.
  - 5+2i ≡ 25 = (−4)^{−1}, so ind = 100 − 4 = 96.
  - 1−10i ≡ 2 = −10·20 ≡ 11^{75}·11^2, so ind = 77.
- All 28 index entries are reproduced by this check.

Modulus m = 9+4i, D = 97:
- i ≡ −9·4^{−1} ≡ 22 (mod 97), since 22² ≡ −1. So g = 1+i ↦ 23.
- 23 is a primitive root mod 97: 23^24 ≡ 22 = i, 23^48 ≡ −1, 23^32 ≡ 61.
- The powers k = 0..24: 1, 1+i, 2i, −2+2i, −4, 5, −4+i, 4+i, 3+5i, 2−i, 3+i, 2+4i, 2−3i, 5−i, −3, −3−3i, −4+3i, 2+3i, 3−4i, −2−5i, −1+2i, −3+i, −4−2i, −2−6i, i. These map to 1, 23, 44, 42, 93, 5, 18, 26, 16, 77, 25, 90, 33, 80, 94, 28, 62, 68, 12, 82, 43, 19, 49, 60, 22 mod 97.
- Gauss first wrote a row '25' and struck it, since the cycle ends at 24.
- The index table here is only begun: 14 entries, from i up to 1−6i. Examples:
  - 1+2i ≡ 45 ≡ 23^{33}.
  - −3−2i ≡ 50 ≡ 23^{84}.
  - 1−6i ≡ 63 ≡ 23^{87}.

Purpose: these tables let one read off the biquadratic character directly, since [q/m]_4 ≡ q^{(p−1)/4} = i^{ind q} [my addition]. That supports numerical testing of biquadratic reciprocity and of the character of 1+i, the subject of Theoria residuorum biquadraticorum II (1832). The neighbouring folios hold the same kind of tables for moduli −7+8i, −3+10i, 5+8i, −3+8i and 5+6i.
errors: No arithmetical errors found. All 26 powers and all 28 indices for modulus 1+10i, and all 25 powers and 14 indices for 9+4i, were recomputed and agree.
Not an error: the index table for 9+4i is incomplete. It omits 5±4i, −7, −7±2i, 5±6i, −3±8i, 5±8i, 9−4i and 1±10i, so it was apparently left unfinished.
Not an error: entries 23 and 24 for modulus 1+10i are partly blotted. Arithmetic forces them to be 1+5i and −5−4i.

results.what: Table of powers of the primitive root 1+i and indices (discrete logarithms) of all normalised Gaussian primes of norm ≤ 101, modulo the Gaussian prime 1+10i (norm 101)
results.modern_name: Index table (discrete logarithm table) for a Gaussian prime modulus; Gaussian analogue of a Canon arithmeticus
results.usually_credited_to: Index tables for rational primes: Gauss (Disquisitiones, 1801, small table) and Jacobi, Canon Arithmeticus (1839). The Gaussian-integer theory of primitive roots: Gauss, Theoria residuorum biquadraticorum II (1832).

results.what: Same for modulus 9+4i (norm 97), primitive root 1+i, with a partial index table
results.modern_name: Discrete logarithm table in Z[i]/(9+4i) ≅ F_97

results.what: Implicit use of the index mod 4 as the biquadratic residue character: q^{(N−1)/4} ≡ i^{ind q}
results.modern_name: Quartic (biquadratic) residue symbol via discrete logarithms

deep.surprise_reason: These are routine computational tables from Gauss's well-documented work on biquadratic residues and Gaussian integers. They are correct and carefully made, but contain no new theory. Similar Nachlass tables are known to belong to that research programme.

Modulus 1+10i, power 24: the blotted sign is minus, so the entry is −5−4i (≡ −45 mod 101).
Modulus 9+4i, power table: a struck-out row label '25' follows 24 | +i. It was deleted because the cycle ends at index 24 = 96/4.
Small marks in the left margin beside the 9+4i index rows (+1−i, +1+2i) are stray ticks, not part of the entries.
